steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here’s a concise comparison of DNA and RNA across several key features:

1. Sugar Backbone  
   • DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) contains deoxyribose, which lacks an oxygen atom at the 2′ carbon.  
   • RNA (ribonucleic acid) contains ribose, which has a hydroxyl (–OH) group at the 2′ carbon.  

2. Nitrogenous Bases  
   • Both share adenine (A), guanine (G) and cytosine (C).  
   • DNA uses thymine (T) in place of uracil.  
   • RNA substitutes uracil (U) for thymine.  

3. Strand Structure  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming a stable double helix.  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded and can fold into complex secondary structures (hairpins, loops).  

4. Location and Stability  
   • DNA resides mainly in the cell nucleus (and in mitochondria/chloroplasts). It’s chemically more stable—ideal for long-term genetic information storage.  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus (in eukaryotes) but functions in the cytoplasm. It’s less stable (the extra –OH makes it more prone to hydrolysis), suitable for transient roles.  

5. Function  
   DNA’s primary role:  
     – Store and transmit hereditary information from one generation to the next.  
   Major RNA roles include:  
     – mRNA (messenger RNA): carries genetic code from DNA to ribosomes.  
     – tRNA (transfer RNA): brings amino acids during protein synthesis.  
     – rRNA (ribosomal RNA): core component of ribosomes, catalyzes peptide bond formation.  
     – Other regulatory and catalytic RNAs (siRNA, miRNA, ribozymes, etc.).  

6. Replication vs. Transcription  
   • DNA replication is semi-conservative: each daughter molecule has one old and one new strand.  
   • RNA is made by transcription, copying just one DNA strand into a single RNA molecule.  

7. Longevity and Turnover  
   • DNA persists for the life of the cell (or organism) with repair mechanisms to correct damage.  
   • RNA molecules typically have short half-lives—mRNAs may last minutes to hours; some noncoding RNAs are more stable.  

Summary  
DNA is a double-stranded, deoxyribose-based polymer with thymine, optimized for stable, long-term genetic storage. RNA is a single-stranded, ribose-based polymer with uracil, versatile in form and function—acting as the intermediary and machinery of gene expression.
